title: Demystifying Instruction Mixing for Fine-tuning Large Language Models
extended_summary:
This paper investigates how different types of instruction-tuning data should be mixed when fine-tuning large language models (LLMs). The authors focus on a methodological question in AI model development: whether combining instruction datasets for NLP downstream tasks, coding, and general chat improves overall model performance, and how such mixtures affect different capabilities. The paper is not an education study; rather, it is a machine learning study about the behavior of LLMs under different fine-tuning data mixtures.

The intervention examined is instruction fine-tuning of LLaMA-2 7B and 13B models using three datasets: Alpaca for general chat-style instructions, CodeAlpaca for coding tasks, and P3 for NLP downstream tasks. The authors fine-tune models on all eight combinations of these datasets and evaluate them using zero-shot NLP benchmarks, HumanEval for code generation, and FLASK/GPT-4-based alignment assessments. They also test different mixing ratios and numbers of training instances to better understand how data composition influences outcomes.

The study population is not human learners, teachers, or schools; the units studied are AI models. Experiments were conducted in a computational environment using GPU-based training and benchmark evaluation rather than in classrooms or educational institutions. No educational implementation context, participant demographics, or teaching setting is reported.

The main conclusion is that different instruction types improve the capabilities most closely aligned with their content, but mixing all instruction types does not consistently improve every outcome. P3 improves NLP benchmark performance but can reduce conversational alignment, while CodeAlpaca improves coding and can also support chat-related alignment. General instruction data from Alpaca produces the strongest alignment gains. The authors also conclude that larger models can make better use of diverse instruction mixtures than smaller models, and that instruction ratio and data volume matter for performance.

identified_tools.name: LLaMA 2
identified_tools.description: A named large language model family used as the base model for instruction fine-tuning and evaluation.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper fine-tuned LLaMA-2 7B and 13B on different mixtures of instruction datasets (Alpaca, CodeAlpaca, and P3) to study how instruction mixing affects NLP benchmark performance, code generation, and alignment/chat skills.

findings.finding_summary: On zero-shot NLP benchmarks, instruction mixtures affected LLaMA 2 performance differently by dataset type and model size. For LLaMA-2-7B, P3-only tuning achieved the highest average NLP score (58.2 vs 54.6 baseline), while for LLaMA-2-13B, the CP mixture achieved the best average NLP score (61.9 vs 58.8 baseline). The paper reports that specialized instruction datasets improved performance in their target task areas, but combining all instruction types did not uniformly improve all tasks.
findings.measure: Zero-shot average across ARC, Winogrande, PIQA, MMLU, RACE, and HellaSwag

findings.finding_summary: On code generation, LLaMA 2 improved most when trained with coding data, with gains depending on mixture and model size. For LLaMA-2-7B, AC reached HumanEval pass@1=17.5 and pass@10=25.0 versus C at 16.2 and 24.4 and baseline at 13.7 and 21.3; for LLaMA-2-13B, ACP performed best with pass@1=20.2 and pass@10=32.9 versus baseline 15.4 and 26.2. The authors conclude coding instructions improve coding proficiency and can also benefit broader capabilities.
findings.measure: HumanEval code generation pass@1 and pass@10

findings.finding_summary: For alignment/chat ability assessed with FLASK and GPT-4 scoring, Alpaca-tuned LLaMA 2 showed the strongest standalone alignment results, while adding P3 reduced alignment. LLaMA-2-7B average alignment was 60.6 for A, 61.2 for AC, 45.8 for P, and 59.6 for ACP; LLaMA-2-13B average alignment was 64.0 for A, 65.6 for AC, 47.8 for P, and 61.4 for ACP. The paper states that mixing P3 caused a drop of -2.8 points (7B) and -3.6 points (13B) in alignment skills, whereas combining CodeAlpaca with general instructions improved alignment by +0.6 (7B) and +1.6 (13B).
findings.measure: FLASK alignment skill assessment average score across logical correctness, factuality, commonsense understanding, comprehension, completeness, insightfulness, readability, and conciseness

findings.finding_summary: When varying instruction-mixing ratios for LLaMA-2-7B while holding Alpaca at 20K instances, both NLP benchmark average and HumanEval pass@1 first decreased, then increased, peaking at a specialized-instruction ratio of 1.5 before dropping slightly at 2.0. Performance also plateaued when the number of fine-tuning instances exceeded 10K per instruction type.
findings.measure: Performance sensitivity to instruction-mixing ratio and number of fine-tuning instances

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical ML benchmarking study with controlled experiments, but it is not an education intervention study and does not use RCT/QED causal designs on learners. Outcomes are model benchmark scores and GPT-4-based evaluations rather than student learning measures.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clear performance differences across benchmark and alignment outcomes, but no standardized education effect sizes are provided and some effects are mixed or negative depending on instruction mixture. Impact is therefore evident but unclear in magnitude for education contexts.
